name: Phenylpiracetam (Phenotropil)

lead: Phenylpiracetam is a Soviet-era racetam with a phenyl group added to piracetam. It is prescribed in Russia and sold through gray channels elsewhere.
People take it for energy, drive and reduced fatigue, which supports training and study consistency. Animal work on its S-form reported lower weight gain.

paras: The R-enantiomer inhibits the dopamine transporter and it also binds nicotinic receptors; onset is within an hour and half-life about three to five hours.

Reported effects are insomnia, agitation, flushing and raised blood pressure. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and under 18 in Russian labelling, unapproved in the US and banned in-competition by WADA. Supplement products have been found mislabelled.

angle.text: Users take it for energy and drive on long days and before workouts. Animal studies of its S-form reported lower body weight gain on a Western diet, which some body-composition users cite.[7]

lead: Phenylpiracetam, also called fonturacetam or by the brand Phenotropil, is a stimulant-leaning racetam with a phenyl group added to the piracetam structure. It was developed in the Soviet Union for cosmonauts and first described in 1983.[1][2] People take it for mental energy, motivation and stamina, which supports training, study and long working days; in animal work the S-enantiomer also reduced weight gain, a result that interests some body-composition users.[3]

It is prescribed in Russia, approved there in 2003, for conditions such as cerebrovascular insufficiency, apathy and asthenia.[1][4] In the United States it is an unapproved drug, and it is the only racetam on the WADA prohibited list for in-competition use.[1]

Research is mostly Russian clinical work and animal studies, together with reviews of its pharmacology.[5][6] Studies of purchased supplements have found phenylpiracetam-class racetams sold or mislabelled as nootropic products.[7][8]
infobox: Rx in Russia and Australia; unapproved in US; WADA-prohibited[1]

paras: Users describe taking phenylpiracetam for energy, motivation and pre-workout drive. A 2017 study in mice found that the S-isomer reduced body weight gain without changing locomotor activity.[3]

In Russia it is prescribed for cerebrovascular deficiency, depression, apathy, attention and memory problems, and recovery after brain injury, and as an add-on in epilepsy.[1][4] A 2024 Russian review discusses prospects in cerebral ischemia, neurodegenerative disease, epilepsy, asthenia and metabolic syndrome.[5]

Published human studies are largely Russian and reviewed in Russian-language journals.[5] A 2026 registered phase 1 study lists racetam-class compounds among those used to test IQ-testing reliability in healthy adults.[9] Animal studies report anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects of the R-isomer in mice.[10]

Reported effects include insomnia, agitation, flushing, a feeling of warmth and raised blood pressure; reduced appetite has been noted with extended use.[1] Labels in Russia list pregnancy, breastfeeding and under-18 age as contraindications.[4]
The (R)-enantiomer is a selective dopamine transporter inhibitor, and phenylpiracetam also binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in mouse cortex.[1][10][3]
Oral bioavailability is reported near complete, onset within an hour and half-life of three to five hours, with little metabolism; human pharmacokinetic data are largely unpublished.[1]

The compound was developed at the Institute of Biomedical Problems in Moscow for Soviet space missions and described in 1983.[1][2] It was approved in Russia in 2003.[1] The R-enantiomer was identified as a dopamine reuptake inhibitor in 2014.[1]

It is prescription-only in Russia and Australia, unapproved in the United States, and prohibited by WADA in competition.[1] A 2023 review notes fonturacetam was the first nootropic banned in sport, in 1998.[11]
Studies of online supplements have found unapproved drugs in nootropic products, sometimes at pharmaceutical-level amounts and not always as labelled.[7][8]
